item.research_question: Can high-entropy alloy nanopatterns be synthesized using a DNA origami-based metallization reaction system?
item.material_system: High-entropy multimetallic nanopatterns composed of up to five metal elements (Co, Pd, Pt, Ag, and Ni)
item.processing_route: DNA origami-based metallization reaction system with a one-step or two-step process, using metal ion precursors and reducing agents
item.test_conditions: Room temperature, 1× TA–Mg2+ buffer, and various reducing agents
key_findings: Multimetallic nanopatterns with controlled morphology, composition, and uniformity can be synthesized
The atomic distribution uniformity of multimetallic nanopatterns can be regulated by specific elements
The introduction of Ag leads to a decrease in catalytic activity, while the introduction of Ni leads to enhanced catalytic performance
The CoPdPt nanoalloy has the highest catalytic activity among the tested multimetallic nanoalloys
The KM value for H2O2 is 0.98 mM, indicating a higher affinity to the substrate than horseradish peroxidase
item.mechanism: The strong coordination between metal elements and DNA bases enables the accumulation of metal ions on protruding clustered DNA (pcDNA), which serves as a nucleation site for metal plating
item.limitations: The immiscible nature of some metal elements, such as Ag, can lead to phase separation and inhomogeneous distribution
item.future_work: Developing methodologies for uniformity and phase separation control, and exploring the potential of nanoalloys arrays with specific shapes and components for catalysis
quotes: High-entropy multimetallic nanopatterns with controlled morphology, composition and uniformity hold great potential for developing nanoelectronics, nanophotonics and catalysis
The strong binding of metal precursors facilitates their accumulation around pcDNA and the subsequent metallization
The results may give inspiration to developing methodologies for uniformity and phase separation control

Mechanism: The strong coordination between metal elements and DNA bases enables the accumulation of metal ions on protruding clustered DNA (pcDNA), which serves as a nucleation site for metal plating.
